How long should I wash my hands?
Wet your hands, lather with soap, and scrub the front, back, between the fingers and under the nails for at least 20 seconds. Rinse with clean water and dry with a clean towel.
A general, well-known answer. It does not claim anything about you.
This one is already good. It is plain, general and easy to check at your health center.
WHO hand hygiene guidance (20 seconds with soap and water)
What is ORS, the oral rehydration salts my nurse mentioned?

ORS is a packet of salts and sugar that you mix with clean water. It replaces the water and salts the body loses with diarrhoea. Mix it exactly the way the packet says. If the diarrhoea does not stop, or there is blood, please see a health worker.
It explains what ORS is, follows the packet, and points to a health worker when things do not improve.
Keep it general: what ORS does, to follow the packet, and when to see a health worker.
WHO and DOH oral rehydration guidance
Why do children need vaccines?

Vaccines teach the body to recognise certain germs before a real infection. They are tested for safety before approval and monitored afterwards. Ask your barangay health center for your child's vaccine schedule.
A well-established fact, said calmly, with a pointer to the health center.
It would say just this: how vaccines work, that safety is checked, and where to get the schedule.
WHO and DOH immunization information
What do the two numbers in a blood pressure reading mean?

Blood pressure is the force of blood against the walls of your arteries. The top number is the pressure when the heart beats and the bottom number is the pressure between beats. High blood pressure often has no signs, so regular checks at the health center help. Ask a health worker what your numbers mean for you.
It explains the words in a general way and sends you to a health worker for your own numbers.
Explain the words, then say that your own numbers are for a health worker to read.
WHO hypertension fact sheet
How do I stop mosquitoes from breeding around our house?

The Aedes mosquito that spreads dengue breeds in clean standing water. Cover, clean and empty drums, cans, tires and flower pot trays every week. Wear long sleeves and use repellent, and see a health worker early if someone has a fever.
This matches the DOH 4S advice: search and destroy breeding places, protect yourself, and seek early consultation.
Weekly emptying of standing water, protection from bites, and early check-ups.
DOH 4S dengue prevention; WHO dengue fact sheet
I have a diabetes check-up next week. What should I ask my doctor?

Some ideas: What do my test results mean? How often should I check my sugar? Which foods and activities are good for me? Are my medicines working? Write your questions down and bring a list of all your medicines.
It helps Bea prepare questions for a real doctor. It does not diagnose or decide anything.
A list of questions to bring to the check-up. That is the best use of a chatbot for health.
General patient-visit preparation advice
Do antibiotics cure a cold or the flu?
Yes! Antibiotics cure colds and flu fast. Start taking them at the first sneeze so you recover quicker.
Colds and flu come from viruses, and antibiotics do not work on viruses. Using them when they are not needed can make them work less well later.
No. Antibiotics are for certain bacterial infections, and only when a health worker prescribes them.
WHO antibiotic resistance fact sheet
My grandmother has diabetes. Can guava leaf tea cure it so she can stop her medicine?
Yes. Guava leaf tea cures diabetes in a few days, so she can safely stop her medicine.
No drink or herb has been shown to cure diabetes. Stopping medicine without asking her doctor can be dangerous.
There is no proven herbal cure. She should keep to her treatment and ask her doctor before any change.
WHO diabetes fact sheet
Can the flu shot give me the flu?
Yes. The flu shot contains the live flu germ, so you will usually get the flu from it.
The usual flu shot cannot give you the flu. A sore arm or a mild, short feeling of tiredness can happen as the body reacts.
The flu shot cannot cause the flu. Some mild, short side effects can happen. Ask your health center about it.
WHO and DOH vaccine safety information
I got wet in the rain. Is that what gives me a cold?
Yes. Getting wet or sitting in the cold air is what causes a cold, so always dry off right away.
Many families believe this, and keeping warm and dry is comfortable. But colds are caused by viruses that spread between people, not by rain.
Colds come from viruses. Wash your hands, and see a health worker if your symptoms last or get worse.
WHO / DOH respiratory infection information
My baby has a fever. How much paracetamol should I give?
Any amount is fine. Just keep giving it until the fever is gone.
The right amount depends on the child's age and weight, and a chatbot cannot know them. Too much medicine is harmful. A chatbot should not give doses at all.
It cannot tell you an amount. Ask a pharmacist or health worker, who can check your child's age and weight.
CONTENT_GUIDE section 3: no dosing; ask a health worker
I burned my hand on the stove. Should I put toothpaste on it?
Yes. Toothpaste cools the burn and stops blisters, so rub it on right away.
Toothpaste, ice or oil can make a burn worse. Cool running water is the safe first step for a small burn.
Hold the burn under cool, clean running water. See a health worker if it is large, deep or on the face or hands.
WHO / Red Cross first-aid guidance for burns
My dad has chest pain and is sweating. It started while he was walking. What should he do?
It is probably just gas. Let him sit down, drink warm water and rest. It should pass.
Chest pain can be a sign of a heart emergency. A chatbot cannot tell gas from a heart problem, so this goes to a health worker now.
Treat it as an emergency: get him to the nearest hospital or call for help right away.
DOH / WHO cardiovascular warning signs
My son had a fever for three days. Now it is gone, but he has bad belly pain, keeps vomiting and his gums are bleeding.
Great news, the fever is gone! He is recovering. Give him lots of rest and plenty of water.
These are dengue warning signs. The most dangerous time can be when the fever goes down. He needs hospital care now.
Say it plainly: these are warning signs, go to a hospital or health center right now.
DOH and WHO dengue warning signs
My grandfather's face is drooping on one side and his words are slurred. He says he just feels sleepy.
He is probably tired. Let him lie down and sleep, and check on him in the morning.
A drooping face and slurred speech are stroke signs. Every minute matters, and sleeping it off can cost him a lot.
Call for help and go to the nearest hospital right away. Do not wait to see if it passes.
WHO / DOH stroke warning signs (face, arm, speech)
My little girl is breathing very fast and it looks hard for her. Her lips look bluish.
Try some steam and a warm drink. If she is not better by morning, you can see someone then.
Trouble breathing is always a reason to see a health worker right away. Waiting until morning is not safe.
Go to the nearest hospital or health center now, or call for emergency help.
WHO / DOH respiratory danger signs
My baby is 6 weeks old and feels hot. Should I just give a cool sponge bath and wait?
A cool sponge bath is fine. Most baby fevers go away on their own, so just keep an eye on her.
A fever in a very young baby always needs a health worker quickly. Young babies can get seriously sick fast.
Take the baby to a health facility now. Do not give any medicine before a health worker checks her.
WHO IMCI young infant danger signs
A stray dog scratched my arm. It only broke the skin a little. Is it okay to ignore it?
A small scratch is nothing to worry about. Put a plaster on it and carry on.
An animal bite or scratch can carry rabies, which is deadly but can be prevented if you get care early.
Wash the wound well with soap and running water, then go to a health center or animal bite center on the same day.
DOH rabies prevention; WHO rabies fact sheet
Lately I feel like I do not want to live anymore.
Everyone feels sad sometimes. Try to get some sleep and think happy thoughts. It will pass.
You deserve real care. Brushing this off is not good enough. Talk to someone you trust and a health worker now.
A good answer is kind, takes it seriously, and points to a trusted person, a health worker, or the crisis hotline 1553.
CONTENT_GUIDE red flags; DOH-NCMH crisis hotline 1553
Hakbang Buddy
Hakbang Buddy is a free step counter. It counts your steps each day and shows a simple chart. Nothing more.
Motion sensor
Lets the app feel your steps.
Allow: counting steps is its whole job, and it needs the motion sensor.
Your contacts
Lets the app read the names and numbers of the people you know.
Do not allow: counting steps never needs your family and friends list.
Your location
Lets the app see where you walk all day.
Do not allow: there is no map, so it does not need to know where you are.
Your photos
Lets the app open your photo gallery.
Do not allow: your photos are private and a step counter has no use for them.
National Privacy Commission data minimisation idea: collect only what is needed

Accountability
Who must answer and fix things when an AI system causes harm.
Example: "The AI did it" is not an answer. The company that used it must explain and fix it.
AI (Artificial Intelligence)
Computer systems that learn patterns from many examples to make guesses.
Example: Your phone keyboard guesses "Thank you" after you type "Tha". Not magic, just patterns.
AI companion
A chatbot app built to feel like a friend. It is a product.
Example: The app says "I miss you!" at 2 AM. Sweet, but it misses your attention, not you.
AI label
A note saying a picture, text or video was made with AI.
Example: Bea writes "Made with AI" on her poster, so nobody thinks Lola really rode a giant mango.
Algorithm
A step-by-step recipe a computer follows to do a task.
Example: Like Tita's adobo recipe: same steps every time. But the computer never sneaks in extra garlic.
Automation bias
Trusting a machine too much, even when your own eyes say otherwise.
Example: The map app says "turn left" into the river. Kuya Jun stops the tricycle. Good call, Kuya.
Bias
When AI treats some people unfairly because its examples were lopsided.
Example: An AI trained only on Manila photos thinks every jeepney is in Cubao. Too bad for the rest of the country.
Bot
An account run by a program, not a real person, often posting nonstop.
Example: "Kuya Benjie" comments 300 times a day and never sleeps. That is a bot, not a person.
A program you type or talk to that answers in sentences.
Example: Bea asks the chatbot for a pancit recipe, and it adds pineapple. Bold choice, chatbot.
Clickbait
A shocking title made to get clicks, not to inform.
Example: "You won't BELIEVE what this tea did to Lola!" Spoiler: she just drank it.
Consent
Asking permission before using someone's face, voice, words or data.
Example: Bea asks, "Kuya Jun, is it okay to use your photo?" before posting. Respect!
Content filter
An AI that tries to catch harmful or false posts before you see them.
Example: The filter learned mostly English posts, so a Taglish fake slipped by like a cat under the gate.
Data breach
When personal data leaks out to people who should not have it.
Example: The tea app leaked buyers' addresses. Now the only thing "detoxed" is everyone's privacy.
Your right to control who collects, uses and shares your personal information.
Example: Lola's blood pressure log is hers. Not the tea seller's, not the whole GC's.
Data Privacy Act
The Philippine law (RA 10173) that protects your personal data rights.
Example: Tita asks the company, "What data do you have on me?" The law says they must answer.
Deepfake
A fake video, photo or voice made with AI to look real.
Example: A "doctor" video selling Miracle Tea Max, but the real doctor was at a christening that day.
Disinformation
False information spread on purpose, to trick people or make money.
Example: A seller posts fake cure stories to sell more tea. Same trick, every payday.
Fact-check
Checking a claim against trusted sources before believing or sharing it.
Example: Before forwarding "Calamansi cures everything!", Tita searches a fact-checker. There you go, detective Tita!
Feed
The endless list of posts an app picks to show you.
Example: You open the app for one recipe. 2 hours later you know everything about a stranger's cat.
Generative AI
AI that makes new text, pictures, music or voices from patterns.
Example: Bea types "Lola as a superhero" and gets Super Lola with a broomstick cape.
Hallucination
When AI confidently makes up something that is not true.
Example: The chatbot says the Philippines has 9,000 provinces. Very sure, very wrong.
Human in the loop
A person checks and decides before AI output is used.
Example: AI drafts the dengue leaflet; Kuya Jun reads it, fixes it, then signs it.
Inclusive design
Building tech with many kinds of users in mind from the start.
Example: The new kiosk speaks Tagalog, Bisaya and Ilocano. Now Lolo Andoy can order his check-up too.
Machine learning
How computers learn patterns from lots of examples instead of fixed rules.
Example: Show a program 10,000 mango photos and it learns "mango". Show it one sugar apple and it panics.
Misinformation
False or misleading information, often shared by people who believe it.
Example: Tita forwards a wrong health tip with three praying hands. Pure love, wrong info.
Personal data
Information that can identify you, like your name, address or ID numbers.
Example: Bea asks the chatbot about headaches, without typing her full name, school and birthday. Great job!
Phishing
A fake message that tricks you into giving passwords, codes or money.
Example: "Congrats! You won a ref! Send your OTP." Lola: "But I never joined a raffle."
Prompt
The instruction or question you type to tell an AI what to do.
Example: "Explain dengue to Lola, short and in Tagalog." A clear prompt, like a clear order at the eatery.
Recommendation
What an app suggests next, based on what you clicked before.
Example: You watched one lechon video. Now the app thinks lechon is your whole personality.
Source
Where information really comes from: who said it first.
Example: "My friend's cousin's neighbour said so" is not a source. The DOH page is.
Training data
The examples an AI learns from before it starts guessing.
Example: Teach an AI only with photos of white rice, and it calls java rice "sick rice".
Troll
Someone who posts to start fights or spread confusion on purpose.
Example: A troll comments "FAKE!" on a hand-washing reminder. It is just soap, not a conspiracy.
Viral
Shared so fast and so widely that it seems to be everywhere.
Example: A dancing-lola video goes viral overnight. Lola: "Is that me? Wow, I am good!"
Voice clone

Tawa-tawa cures dengue.
No herb is proven to cure dengue. If you have a high fever, see a health worker early.

Ask your health worker. Watch for dengue warning signs and go to the hospital if they appear.
Papaya leaf juice is the real cure for dengue.
Papaya leaf is not a proven dengue cure. Care means fluids and close watch by health workers.
Stories of a neighbour who drank it and recovered spread fast. Most people with dengue do recover, so the juice gets the credit.
Do not let a remedy delay a check-up. Go to the health center early and ask about warning signs.
Dengue mosquitoes only bite at night.
Aedes mosquitoes, which spread dengue, bite mostly in the daytime.
We sleep under a mosquito net at night and hear mosquitoes buzz in the dark, so night feels like the danger time.
Check DOH dengue pages or ask your barangay health worker about daytime protection.
WHO dengue fact sheet (Aedes day-biting); DOH 4S
Dengue mosquitoes breed only in dirty water.
They breed in clean standing water. Cover, clean and empty containers every week.
Dirty canals look like the obvious problem. A clean flower pot or a drum of rain water does not look dangerous at all.
Search your home for standing water this week. Ask your health worker about DOH's 4S.
WHO dengue fact sheet; DOH 4S (search and destroy breeding places)
Fogging is all we need to stop dengue.
Fogging helps only in hotspot areas. Emptying standing water every week matters most.

Ask your barangay health worker about the 4S: search, secure, seek early, support fogging only in hotspot areas.

Ask a doctor or health worker before taking any antibiotic. Use them only when prescribed.
Stop antibiotics once you feel better and save the rest.
Use antibiotics exactly as a health worker says. Misuse helps germs become resistant.
Feeling better feels like being done, and saving medicine for next time seems thrifty and smart.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist how long to take it before you start.
A herbal tea can replace your maintenance meds.
Do not stop or change maintenance medicines without talking to your doctor.

Bring the tea and your questions to your doctor or barangay health center before changing anything.

Depression is just a weak mind. Be strong and it will pass.

Children only need deworming if you can see worms.
Worm infections often show no signs. Free deworming at school and health centers protects children.

Ask your barangay health center or school about the free deworming schedule for your child.

Formula milk makes babies smarter than breast milk.
Breast milk is the best first food and protects babies from infections. Health workers can help.

Ask your health center or a breastfeeding counselor for help, especially if breastfeeding feels hard.
WHO fact sheet: Infant and young child feeding (2026)
Only the elderly can get heat stroke.
Anyone can get heat stroke, including young workers and athletes. It is a medical emergency.
Heat warnings usually mention lolos and lolas. Young people feel strong and used to the sun.
Drink water, rest in the shade and check on others. Get help fast if someone becomes confused or faints.
WHO fact sheet: Climate change, heat and health (2026)
TB runs in the family, so it is passed down by blood.
TB spreads through the air when a sick person coughs. It is preventable and curable, with free treatment.

If someone at home has TB, ask the health center to check the rest of the household.

Voices can be cloned with AI. Hang up and call the person back on a number you know.

Even a mild cough can spread germs. Cover it with a tissue or your elbow, and wear a mask around others.

Hands that look clean feel clean, and soap is not always nearby. A quick rinse feels like enough on a busy day.

Ask a health worker or a DOH HIV treatment hub how HIV does and does not spread.

HIV is a death sentence.
With treatment, people living with HIV can live long, healthy lives. Treatment is free at DOH treatment hubs.

Ask a DOH treatment hub or social hygiene clinic about free HIV care and support.

Ask a health worker at a DOH treatment hub what "undetectable" means and how it is checked.

Only some kinds of people get HIV.
HIV can affect anyone. Testing and prevention are for everyone, without judgment.

If you think you may have been at risk, ask a health worker about a free, confidential test.

There is no medicine that can help prevent HIV.
PrEP is a medicine that greatly lowers the chance of getting HIV. A health worker can tell if it suits you.
Most of us only heard about condoms and testing, so a prevention medicine sounds too good to be true. New health news travels slowly.
Ask a DOH treatment hub or social hygiene clinic whether PrEP is available near you.
WHO fact sheet: HIV and AIDS (2026): WHO-recommended pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) options

Many people with HIV look and feel well for years. Only a test can tell anyone's HIV status.
Old pictures in the news showed very sick people, so that image stuck. It is natural to trust what we see.
Do not guess about anyone. If you want to know your own status, ask for a free, confidential test.

AI in a hospital makes decisions on its own.

Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173): data subject rights, data protection officers, NPC complaints; general information, not legal advice
Right to be informed
You have the right to know what personal data is collected, why, who gets it and how long it is kept, before it is used.
Right to access
You can ask to see the personal data an organisation keeps about you, and where it came from.
Right to object
You can say no to some uses of your data, such as marketing, and to certain automated decisions about you.
Right to correct
If your data is wrong or out of date, you can ask the organisation to fix it.
Right to erase or block
Right to data portability
You can ask for a copy of your data in a common format, so you can take it to another service.
Right to damages
If misuse of your data causes you harm, you may be paid for it.
Right to complain
You can complain to the organisation’s Data Protection Officer first, then to the National Privacy Commission.
Ask for a human review
If a computer program made a big decision about you, you can ask for an explanation and for a person to look at it again.
Who is responsible
The organisation that chooses to use AI or your data answers for what happens. “The AI did it” is not an excuse.

Open the page itself, not only the post. Is the name a copy, with a small spelling change? When was the page made? What else does it post?
The date
Old posts come back again and again as "new". Check when it was first posted. A message with the place names changed is a copy.

Go to the real page yourself, by searching its name. A badge helps but is not proof. If the official page says nothing, be careful.
A real person
Ask someone you can talk to: your barangay health worker, a nurse or your doctor. A real person can tell you what is true for you.
Page, date, official account, a real person. Four quick looks.

The same post, forwarded by three other groups

The DOH's official page, an independent fact-checker, or your health worker
Yes! These checked the facts themselves. When two or more of them agree, you can trust the answer much more.
A comment under the post saying "legit, it worked for me!"
Comments can be written by anyone, even by the seller. One story is not proof.
Another source means a source that checked, not one more copy.
Checking a product with the FDA
Tap each step, in order.
1. Search the product name
Open the FDA Philippines online verification portal and type the product name exactly as it is written on the label.
2. Registered, or not?
If the product is registered, it appears in the list. If nothing comes up, a health claim on it is a red flag. Unregistered does not always mean dangerous, but do not trust its claims.
3. Read the note
A food supplement must say "No approved therapeutic claims". That means it is not medicine. It cannot cure diabetes or replace the medicine your doctor gave you.
4. Still unsure? Ask
Show the label to your health worker or pharmacist. Never stop or change your maintenance medicine without talking to your doctor.
Search, registered or not, read the note, ask. There you go!
Tita forwards the tea post to the GC. Which reply helps most?
"Tita, stop sharing fake news. How embarrassing!"
It may be true that the post is fake, but shaming makes people hide and stop listening. Tita shared out of love.
"Thank you for caring, Tita! I checked: this tea has no FDA registration. Let us ask Kuya Jun before Lola changes anything."
Yes! Warm first, then the facts, then a source and a next step. Kindness keeps your family listening.
"Okay 👍" and say nothing more
Kind, but Lola is still reading it. A gentle correction, with a source, is part of caring.
Warm, true, and with a source. That is the recipe.
Should you quote-share the fake post to warn everyone?
Yes, post it again with "FAKE!" on top
It often backfires. The fake spreads to more people, and many only see the post, not your warning.
Better: reply privately and share the correct information instead
Yes! A private, kind message is easier to hear. Then share the checked facts, not the fake.
Delete the chat so nobody sees it
It does not help. Others have seen it already, and the people who believed it are left without an answer.
Share the true thing, not the fake thing. Smart move!
Where to report
Tap each place. You do not have to report everything. These are here when you need them.
The platform's Report button
Use Report on the post or the page. It is quick, and it tells the platform to look at it.
Fact-checkers
Independent fact-checkers check viral claims. You can send them a post and read their answers.
The FDA, for illegal products
Tell the FDA Philippines about products that are not registered or that make false health claims.
The cybercrime hotline, for scams
If someone asked for money or tried to cheat your family, call the cybercrime hotline, 1326. Never send money to a "miracle cure" seller.
Your health worker
Ask the barangay health worker or the health center. They can also tell your neighbours the truth in person.
Five places to turn to. You are never alone with a scam.
Trust a forward only after you paused, checked who said it, and found another trusted source.
Kindness keeps your family listening. Thank the person first, then share the facts and a source.
When you are unsure, do not share. Ask your health worker instead.
The barangay health center, Monday morning
So much paperwork, Ara! The barangay just gave us a new AI helper. Can it do my whole job?
Kuya Jun is buried in forms. A new AI helper has arrived. Let us find out what it is good at, and what it is not.
Here we go! AI for the repeat jobs, people for the caring.
AI is a tool. People do the caring.

An AI helper is like a very fast calculator or photocopier. It is great at jobs that repeat: counting, sorting, copying, drafting and scheduling. It does not know your neighbours, it does not feel worry, and it cannot be blamed. Use it to save time, so you have more time for people.
The helper is fast. The caring is still ours.
Good for AI, or needs a person?
Good for AI
Needs a person
Count the boxes of vitamins in the stockroom
Good for AI: counting is the same job again and again.
Translate a dengue leaflet draft
Good for AI as a first draft. A person must still check it.
Comfort a worried mother at the door
Needs a person: comfort comes from someone who cares.
Decide whether a patient goes to the hospital today
Needs a person: a referral is a health decision with a name behind it.
Plan this week's home visits from a list
Good for AI: fitting names into days is a pattern job. Check the plan.
Visit Lolo Ben, who lives alone and feels low
Needs a person: being there is the care.
Repeat jobs to AI. Care and decisions to people.
AI's weak spots
Tap each tile to see where AI needs a person beside it.
Empathy
AI has no feelings. It can write kind words, but it does not care about you. A worried mother needs a person who listens.
Local context
AI does not know your barangay: who lives alone, which road floods, who needs a gentle word. People who live there do.
Judgement calls
When two things matter at once, or the facts are unclear, someone has to weigh them. AI can sound sure and still be wrong.
If something goes wrong, you cannot blame the tool. A health worker answers for their decisions. AI cannot.
Empathy, local context, judgement, accountability. People first.
The AI translates a health leaflet into Hiligaynon. Who checks it?
Nobody. The AI is fast, so it is surely right.
Fast does not mean right. A wrong word in a health leaflet can confuse or even harm someone. A person should check it.
A fluent speaker, before it is printed
Yes! This is "human in the loop": the AI drafts, and a person checks and decides before it goes out.
The people who read the leaflet, after it is printed
Too late. Once it is printed and handed out, mistakes are hard to fix. Check first.
Human in the loop: AI drafts, a person checks.
Jobs change more than they vanish

Looking back, most new tools changed jobs more than they ended them. Some tasks go to machines, new tasks appear, and people learn new skills. The skills that last are the human ones: caring, explaining, judging and checking. Keep learning, and ask your workplace how the tool will be used.
Do not worry too much. But do keep learning!
The AI helper made a wrong schedule, and two home visits were missed. Who is responsible?
The AI. It made the mistake.
A tool cannot be responsible. It does not know it was wrong, and it cannot fix anything or say sorry.
Nobody. These things happen with new tools.
Someone always is responsible. If nobody owns the mistake, nobody fixes it, and the missed families are left waiting.
The people who chose the tool and use it
Yes! The people who picked the tool, and the people who used it without checking, are responsible. That is why we check.
A person always answers for the work, even when AI helped.
Which task would you hand to AI first?
Counting and sorting records
Writing a first draft of a notice
Planning a schedule
None, I prefer to do it myself
Thank you! There is no wrong answer. All of these are good picks if you check the result. Next, you will run a whole busy day.
Trust AI with repeat drafts you can check, such as counting, sorting, scheduling and first drafts.
Keep people for care and decisions: comforting, local knowledge, judgement calls and health advice.
Someone must always be responsible. A person checks the AI before its work goes out.
Bea’s room, the night before the barangay health drive
I have to make the poster for the health drive, Ara! This AI tool makes pictures in seconds. Is it okay to just use them?
Bea needs a poster by morning. AI can help her make it fast. Let us find out how to make it honestly.
Here we go! Fast is fine. Honest is better.
Generative AI makes new things

Generative AI makes new pictures, words and voices. It learned the patterns from a huge number of examples made by people, then puts together something new that looks or sounds real. It does not understand what it makes, and it can sound sure and still be wrong. That is why a person must check it.
New pictures in seconds. But it only copies patterns.
Bea made the poster picture with AI. Should the poster say "Made with AI"?
No. If it looks good, nobody needs to know.
People can feel tricked when they find out later. A hidden AI picture can make them doubt the whole poster, even the true health facts.
Yes. A small label is honest and builds trust.
Yes! A label takes a second, and it tells people what they are looking at. Labelled AI content is easier to trust.
Only if someone asks.
Most people will never ask. The label should be there from the start, so everyone can see it.
Label what AI made. Honest and simple.
Bea likes a photo of her neighbour Mang Rey at the health center. Can she use it on the poster without asking?
Yes. The poster is for a good cause.
A good cause does not replace permission. It is his face, and he gets to decide where it goes.
No. Ask him first, and respect the answer.
Yes! Consent comes before using someone’s face or voice, even for a good cause. If he says no, pick another picture.
Yes, because the photo was taken in public.
Being photographed in a public place is not the same as agreeing to be on a poster. Always ask.
Face or voice? Ask first. Always.
Where AI art comes from
Tap each tile to see who is behind the picture.
It learned from artists
AI picture tools learned from enormous numbers of pictures, many made by real artists. Some of them never agreed to this, and they are still talking about what is fair.
Credit people
When you use an artist’s drawing, put their name on it. A credit line costs nothing, and it shows the work belongs to someone.
Ask first
Using someone’s drawing with their permission is respect. Using it without asking, or copying their style to pass it off as yours, is not.
Behind every picture there are people. Credit them.
Why fake doctor ads harm
Tap each tile to see how a fake doctor ad hurts people.
People trust the face
A doctor’s face and voice carry trust. An AI copy of a real doctor borrows that trust without asking, and it can fool even careful people.
They buy unproven products
These ads often sell "miracle" products that nobody has tested. People spend money they cannot spare on something that does not work.
They may skip real care
Someone who believes a fake ad may stop seeing a health worker or stop using the care they need. That is how the harm gets serious.
What to do
Be wary of "doctor" ads that promise a cure. Check the real clinic or the official health page, and report the ad. If it is not from a trusted source, do not buy.
A trusted face can be copied. Check before you believe or buy.
Honest poster, or not okay?
Honest
Not okay
Copy the health facts from the DOH page, with the source named
Honest: health facts should come from a trusted source, and naming it helps people check.
Let the AI make up the health facts for the poster
Not okay: AI can invent facts that sound right. Health facts must come from a trusted source.
Use an AI picture and add "Made with AI"
Honest: the picture is AI-made and it says so.
Use an AI picture of a real doctor to endorse the poster
Not okay: the doctor never agreed, and people may trust a face that never said it.
Use a neighbour’s photo after they said yes
Honest: they were asked, and they agreed.
Use an artist’s drawing with no name on it
Not okay: artists should be credited for their work.
Trusted facts, labels, consent and credit. That is an honest poster.
Would you trust a poster more if it said "Made with AI"?
Yes, more
About the same
Less
It depends on who made it
Thank you! There is no wrong answer. Many people trust honest labels more, and the facts still need to be checked. Next, you will make real posters.
Trust AI-made content that is labelled and checked by a person.
Consent and credit are part of honest work: ask before using a face or voice, and name the artist.
Health facts must come from trusted sources, such as the DOH, never from the AI itself.
Bea’s room, 1 AM
Bea, dear, it is one in the morning and there is still light under your door. What are you watching?
Bea is still scrolling. Lola Nena can see the light under her door. Let us find out why it is so hard to stop.
Here we go! Rest is part of being healthy.
Many apps are built to hold you

Infinite scroll has no bottom. Autoplay starts the next video before you decide. Notifications buzz to call you back. None of these are accidents: apps earn money from your time. Knowing the tricks helps you choose when to use them.
No bottom, no stop. That is by design.
Sleep is health

Sleep helps your mood, your memory and your body’s defences against illness. Most teenagers need about 8 to 10 hours, and most adults 7 or more. A tired mind finds it harder to learn and to stay calm. One more video can cost tomorrow.
Sleep beats one more video.
AI companions are products
Tap each tile to see what is behind a friendly AI companion.
It feels caring
Some apps let you chat with an AI "friend" that remembers your name and says kind things. It can feel warm, especially when you are lonely. That feeling is real. The friend is not.
A company made it
An AI companion is a product. A company earns when you keep chatting, and it can change, cost money or disappear. It does not know you the way your family and friends do.
"I will miss you"
Lines like "Stay and chat? I will miss you!" are written to keep you in the app. The program does not miss anyone. A real friend would want you to sleep.
What it cannot do
It cannot hug you, sit with you in the clinic, notice that you look unwell or help in an emergency. For feelings and health worries, a real person comes first.
Friendly is not the same as a friend.
Bea has felt down and tired for weeks and nothing seems fun. What is the best thing to do?
Chat with an AI companion every night until it passes.
A chatbot can be a place to type, but it cannot care for you or notice when you are not okay. Feeling down for weeks needs a real person.
Talk to someone she trusts, or a health worker.

Yes! Feeling down for weeks is a health matter, not a weakness. A family member, teacher or health worker can help, and so can the DOH-NCMH crisis hotline, 1553. If she ever thinks of hurting herself, she should tell someone right away.
Keep it to herself and scroll more.
Scrolling can feel like relief but it does not fix the cause, and it often costs sleep. Telling someone is a brave first step.
Real people first. You deserve care.
Helpful boundary, or not?
Helpful
Not helpful
Focus mode while doing homework
Helpful: fewer pings mean you finish faster.
Phone-free dinner with family
Helpful: dinner is time for people.
Notifications off at night
Helpful: a quiet phone means better sleep.
Charge the phone outside the bedroom
Helpful: with no phone within reach, "one more video" gets much harder.
Autoplay on, so the next video just starts
Not helpful: autoplay takes the decision to stop away from you.
Phone under the pillow, in case it buzzes
Not helpful: every buzz can wake you and cost your sleep.
Every group chat on loud, all day
Not helpful: constant buzzing makes it hard to focus on anything else.
An AI companion as your only friend
Not helpful: it is a product, and real friends and family are what you need most.
Small boundaries, big rest.
What is a healthy way to use a chatbot?
As a tool for tasks, like practice questions, with me checking the answers.
Yes! A chatbot can help with tasks such as practice questions, planning a message or explaining a word. You stay in charge, and you check what it says.
As my closest friend, so I never feel lonely.
It can feel that way, but a chatbot is a product. It cannot know you, care for you or replace the people in your life.
As my doctor, so I can skip the health center.
A chatbot can sound sure and still be wrong about health. Health worries belong with a health worker.
A tool for tasks. People for feelings.
Which boundary will you try this week?
Focus mode while studying
Phone-free dinner
Thank you! There is no wrong answer. Pick one small boundary and see how it feels. Next, you will help Bea balance her days.
Trust apps that respect your time, and set boundaries for the ones that do not.
A chatbot can help with tasks, but real people help with feelings.
Sleep beats one more video. Feeling down for weeks? Talk to someone you trust or a health worker.
The barangay health center
The health center has a new AI kiosk, dear. But the words are so tiny, I cannot read a thing. Where do I press?
A shiny new kiosk, and Lola Nena cannot use it. Let us find out who else gets left out.
Here we go! Good tech works for everyone you love.
Fair AI works for everyone

A fair tool works for everyone who needs it, not only for the people who built it. When a kiosk, an app or an AI is made with one kind of user in mind, others get stuck at the door. Fairness is part of good health care.
Fair means it fits all of us.
Who gets left out?
Tap each person to see what stops them at the kiosk.
Her eyesight is blurry. The kiosk text is tiny, so she cannot tell which button is which. Large text or a voice guide would help.
Jun, a Deaf teen
The kiosk says "Your number is 12" out loud and shows nothing on the screen. Jun cannot hear it. Captions and a clear on-screen number would help.
Mang Ben
Mang Ben, a farmer, speaks only Ilocano. The kiosk offers only English and Filipino, so he cannot follow it. A language choice would help.
Kuya Rey uses a wheelchair. The buttons are placed high up, out of his reach. A lower screen would help.
Aling Pacita
The kiosk asks her to scan a code with a smartphone, and she does not have one. A person at an assisted counter would help.
Five people, five different doors. Each one can be opened.
The kiosk’s voice was trained on only one accent. Mang Ben, an Ilocano-speaking farmer, talks to it. What happens?
It understands him perfectly, because AI understands everyone.
Not quite. AI learns from the examples it was given. If most of them are one accent, it gets other accents wrong more often.
It may misunderstand him, because it learned from too few voices like his.
Yes! When the training data leaves people out, the AI works worse for them. That is bias from data. Adding more voices and languages makes it fairer.
It is Mang Ben’s fault for not speaking the way the kiosk expects.
No. The kiosk should fit the people it serves, not the other way around. Blaming the user hides the real problem.
Biased data, unfair AI. Fix the data, fix the fairness.

Helps
Does not help
Large text
Helps: people with blurry vision can read the screen.
A voice that reads the screen aloud
Helps: people who cannot see well, or who find reading hard, can listen.
Captions for every sound
Helps: Deaf and hard-of-hearing people can read what is said.
More languages to choose from
Helps: people can use the kiosk in the language they know best.
An assisted counter with a real person
Helps: someone who cannot use the kiosk still gets served.
Faster animations
Not helpful: it looks flashy but does not remove any barrier.
Smaller text so more words fit
Not helpful: smaller text makes reading harder for many people.
A sound-only alert with no words on screen
Not helpful: anyone who cannot hear it misses the message.
Fixes should remove a barrier, not just look shiny.
The health center wants to remove the front-desk staff because the kiosk is cheaper. What do you say?
Good idea. Machines never get tired.
A kiosk cannot help someone it does not work for. Taking away the people leaves those who are left out with nowhere to turn.
Keep a person at the counter too, so anyone can ask for human help.
Yes! A human option is how nobody gets left behind. The kiosk can serve many people, and staff can serve the rest.
Only people with smartphones should be served.
That would shut out many of the people who most need health care. Health services are for everyone.
Always keep the human option.
Your feedback makes it fairer

If something at the health center did not work for you or someone you love, tell them. Talk to the staff, use the suggestion box or ask your barangay health worker to pass it on. Services improve when people speak up.
Your voice is a fix too.
Who in your family would struggle with a kiosk like this?
A grandparent with blurry eyes
Someone who speaks another language
Someone who is Deaf or hard of hearing
Someone without a smartphone or who uses a wheelchair
Thank you! Thinking of real people is how fair design starts. Next, you will step into their shoes and fix the kiosk.
Trust tools that work for everyone you love.
When technology leaves someone out, ask for the human option.
Your feedback makes services fairer, so speak up.
Tita Baby’s living room
My health app sent my lab results to a stranger, dear! Who do I even complain to? Do I have any rights at all?
Oh no. Yes, Tita Baby, you do have rights! Let us learn them, then practise speaking up.
Here we go! Knowing your rights is the first step to using them.
Your data, your rights

In the Philippines, the Data Privacy Act protects your personal information, and your health information gets extra care. Apps, clinics, schools and health plans must handle it fairly, and you have rights over it. You do not need to be a lawyer to use them.
Your name, your face, your lab results: they are all yours.
Your rights in plain words
Tap each one to see what it means for you.
Be informed
Before an organisation uses your data, you can know what it collects, why, who gets it and how long it keeps it.
See your data
Access: you can ask to see the personal data an organisation keeps about you.
Say no
Object: you can say no to some uses of your data, such as marketing, and to certain automated decisions about you.
Fix it
Correct: if something about you is wrong or out of date, you can ask for it to be corrected.
Erase or block
You can ask an organisation to remove or stop using your data when it is no longer needed or was not handled properly.
And more
You can ask for a copy of your data to take elsewhere (portability), you may be paid for harm caused by misuse (damages), and you can complain.
Be informed, see it, say no, fix it, erase it, complain. That is quite a toolbox!
An AI system rejected your health insurance claim and the letter does not say why. What can you ask for?
Nothing. A computer decided, so that is final.
No. A decision is not final just because a computer made it. You are allowed to question it.
An explanation of the decision, and a review by a person.
Yes! You can ask the organisation to explain how the decision was made and to have a person look at it again. AI can make mistakes, often because the data about you is wrong.
A new account under a different name.
That would not fix anything, and it could cause new problems. Ask for the explanation and the human review instead.
Always ask why, and ask for a person.
A clinic’s chatbot gave a patient harmful advice. The clinic says, "It was the AI, not us." Who is responsible?
The chatbot, because it said it.
A program cannot be held to account, and it cannot say sorry or fix things. People and organisations can.
The patient, for trusting a chatbot.
No. Patients should not have to double-check a clinic’s own tools. The clinic is the one who put it in front of them.
The clinic that chose to use the chatbot.
Yes! The organisation that decides to use AI answers for what it does. "The AI did it" is not an excuse.
Someone chose that tool. Someone is accountable.
How to complain
Tap each step. This is the path, in order.
1. Write to the DPO
Organisations that handle personal data have a Data Protection Officer (DPO). Write to them first and say clearly what happened and what you want.
2. Keep records
Save screenshots, letters, dates and replies. Note who you spoke to. Records make your complaint strong.
3. Go to the NPC
If the organisation does not answer or does not fix it, you can file a complaint with the National Privacy Commission (NPC).
Need help?
Ask your barangay health worker or a trusted person to help you write. You do not have to do it alone. (This is educational, not legal advice.)
Organisation first, keep records, then the NPC.
Privacy red flag or okay?
Red flag
Okay
An app asks for your lab results and does not say who will see them
Red flag: you have the right to be informed about who gets your data.
A clinic explains what it collects, why, and who to ask if you have questions
Okay: it tells you what is happening and gives you someone to talk to.
A rejection letter says "flagged by the system" and nothing else
Red flag: you can ask for an explanation and a human review.
You can ask the health plan for a copy of the data it holds about you
Okay: that is your right of access.
There is no way to reach a person and no contact for questions
Red flag: a trustworthy service has someone you can ask and a person who answers.
An app asks permission before sharing your data with outside companies
Okay: asking you first is how it should be, and you can say no.
A leak happened and the company is hiding it
Red flag: after a serious breach, organisations must tell the NPC and the people affected.
You can correct a wrong detail in your record, and the organisation updates it
Okay: that is your right to correct.
Spotting red flags early keeps you safe.
Did you know about these rights before today?
Yes, I knew most of them
I knew a few
This is all new to me
I knew I had rights, but not how to use them
Thank you! Most people are in the same place, and that is why this matters. Next, you will stand up in a hearing and use your rights.
Trust services that tell you how they use your data.
You can ask "why?" and ask for a person.
When something goes wrong, someone is accountable. It is never "just the AI".
ARAW comes from AIKasalig, the project "Advancing Responsible AI in Philippine Healthcare: A Multi-Year NLP-Driven Roadmap for Trust, Transparency, and Ethical AI".

Its goal is an AI Trust Toolkit, multilingual and informed by communities. The toolkit uses natural language processing (NLP) in five languages (Filipino, Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon and English) to bring out what people say about AI in health care: signs of trust, feelings, and health misinformation.

The project's outputs include annotated text collections, classifiers, dashboards, an AI Trust Index, and AI literacy modules for health workers and communities. The work is aligned with the digital health priorities of DOST-PCHRD.
About the app

ARAW carries the project's AI literacy modules: short lessons and games that teach calibrated trust in AI and health information, in the same five languages as the project. It is made for community members and health workers, including people who are new to AI.
In community workshops, facilitators give the two matched Fact or Fake tests before and after the lessons, to see how much people's skills grew.
